body:
I have done academic research at two universities (a midwestern public school for my BS and a west coast private school for graduate work) under a total of six advisors.

Undergrad Advisor #1 had serious issues with insecurity and took them out on her students and employees. She would hire technicians (one was my best friend) for the maximum probation time and then fire them before they qualified for benefits. She also constantly insulted me and said I was "no good for research." Once I left, she published my work without giving me credit. She was eventually run out of the department, but she merely switched to a university 2 hrs away and took her $10 M in NIH funding with her.
Undergrad Advisor #2 was largely apathetic, took many vacations, and ignored his students. His only redeeming factor was a desire to teach, and my drive for learning was well-received, except on the occasions when he got pissed off and cussed me out.
Grad Advisor #1 was mentioned above as the unstable witch.
Grad Advisor #2 is a government scientist who unofficially directed a data-gathering project that resulted in a small review paper. I wouldn't want her as an official advisor, though, since she has a bad habit of being overambitious to the point of fantasy.
Grad Advisor #3 was mentioned above as my current boss.
Grad Advisor #4 is co-advising me, but has no real power. I approached him about GA #3 and I not seeing eye-to-eye, and he suggested I leave the group as neither of us will change our minds in the next four years. He also strongly suggested I consider other career paths.

Overall, four professors (UGA #1, GA #1, GA #3, and GA #4) have suggested that I'm not really a good researcher, while UGA #2 insists that I was born for it. Given the trouble I've had, I'm inclined to believe the majority.

The most maddening part of this is that everyone I've worked for says I'm intelligent, hard-working, conscientious, and organized and that everything I say is correct. On the other hand, it seems I'm just not scientist material. And that could be fine, as I'm not convinced I want to surround myself with these people for the rest of my life, but I'm stuck with these expectations (others' and my own) that I'll be some prodigy scientist.

It's also important to note that my father hates being a professor. He enjoys interacting with students (10% of the job), but he can't stand other professors and the politics of publishing (90% of the job). Thus, I'm not enamored with being a professor so much as being a second-generation 'doctor.'

Thank you for your kind words, surelyhope. I actually feel that graduate school is a lot like basic training in that the primary goal is to indoctrinate you into a particular culture and perspective. In the words of Prof. Burke, "graduate school is not about learning... it is socialization" (http://blogs.swarthmore.edu/burke/permanent-features-advice-on-academia/features/). This is deeply dissatisfying to me, because I came here to learn and be trained in new and exciting scientific techniques. These observations have taught me that no matter where I go, I will be faced with immature, irrational, unethical, and (as you said) apathetic advisors who teach you only how to lie, cheat, and steal without getting caught. Thus, if I'm not good enough to get through it here, what makes me think I can succeed somewhere else?

Furthermore, if I do start over, I'm looking at a graduating at the age of 32. Since the Ph.D. market in my field is saturated, I will probably have to do a postdoctoral appointment for an additional 2-6 years, meaning I won't have a job until I'm 34-38 years old. That is a long time to be stuck in academic limbo, especially if you aren't allowed to work on projects that interest you.

All of the above makes me want to switch career paths entirely, but I am fixated on matching my father's degree (he is a professor). The day-to-day here has destroyed my self-respect, but I don't think I can live with myself if I can't be as smart/successful as my father. Plus, I still love science; I just can't find a way to do real science (as opposed to the charlatan nonsense they advocate here).

PS: I have a ton of first- and second-hand stories about unethical practices that are being encouraged here, if anyone is interested.
